summary:
Allwork.space examines whether the "September Surge" in hiring is real, drawing on Fortune reporting, BLS data, LinkedIn Economic Graph analysis and Indeed Hiring Lab data.

Context: August 2025 payrolls added 162,000 jobs, with June and July revised up by a combined 55,000, and unemployment steady at 4.1%. LinkedIn's Kory Kantenga says seasonally adjusted data hides swings that matter to individuals, and that September consistently sees more job postings than any other month.

LinkedIn's 2025 seasonality analysis finds postings usually peak in spring/early summer (around May) then decline, with a second peak in September and October in the U.S., other English-speaking countries and Nordic countries. U.S. postings in August run 3% below March levels, then rise to 14% above March in September and 11% above in October. Applications, however, peak January to May and decline afterward, creating a fall window with less competition.

Indeed's Job Postings Index also shows a ramp-up around Labor Day as employers prepare for Q4 and the holidays, notably in retail and transportation/warehousing, but economist Cory Stahle cautions the bump is typically small. September still benefits from the end of the summer vacation slowdown for hiring managers and HR.

Timing varies by field: accounting postings jumped about 21% from July to August last year; finance and professional services recruit in September and October for start dates the following summer. LinkedIn finds hiring and job transitions peak July to September, drop in December, and rise in January.

Market conditions remain weak: LinkedIn's hiring rate rose just 2% from July to August and hiring is more than 20% below pre-pandemic levels, with jobs per applicant down 6% year over year. Openings were 7.3 million in July versus roughly 7.1 million a year earlier, but employers are slower to extend offers. Kantenga describes a "big crisis of confidence" among job seekers, especially Gen Z. Labor force participation rose to 61.6% in August from 61.4%.
